summary: Help 6–7 year olds find the unknown whole number in addition/subtraction equations where the unknown appears in any position (8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □). The target is a flexible method built on reading '=' as 'both sides balance' and choosing the inverse move, not an 'add the two numbers I can see' habit. Vary the unknown's position deliberately (result, change, start, answer-on-left) and insist on checking by substituting the answer back.
misconceptions: Adding the two visible numbers regardless of the box's position (8 + ? = 11 → 19).
Reading answer-left forms as backwards (5 = □ − 3 → writes 2, i.e. 5 − 3).
Always subtracting or always adding by keyword rather than by the unknown's role.
Not checking the solution by putting it back into the equation.
Treating '=' as 'work out the total' so a box before '=' is confusing.

activities.title: Balance the unknown with counters
steps: Set out an equation with a box, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, on a two-pan balance or bar model where one side already shows 5.
Add or remove counters in the box until both sides match: too few and the box side is too light, too many and it tips down.
State the value that makes both sides balance (for 5 = □ − 3 the box must hold 8, because □ − 3 has to equal 5).
Repeat with the unknown in every position: 8 + ? = 11, □ + 6 = 12, 6 + 6 = □.
Check each solved equation by putting the found number back in and confirming both sides match.
activities.insight: The box holds whatever value makes the two sides equal; '=' means balance, so an answer-on-left form like 5 = □ − 3 is not 'backwards' — it is the same balancing task. One balancing method works for every position.

activities.title: Solve by the inverse, then check
steps: Given □ + 9 = 14, convert it to the inverse: 14 − 9, and compute □ = 5.
Given 8 + ? = 11, use 11 − 8 = 3 rather than guessing and testing values.
Use a fact-family triangle (whole 14; parts 9 and 5) to pick the operation needed for the unknown's position.
Substitute the answer back and confirm the sentence is true.
Practise a mixed set covering result-unknown, change-unknown, start-unknown and answer-left forms.
activities.insight: Once you know which quantity is the whole and which is a part, you can go straight to the answer with the inverse operation instead of slow trial-and-error.

activities.title: Explain your move (strategy talk)
steps: Solve a varied-position equation aloud, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, then explain how you decided what to do.
Answer probes: 'Which of these could you check with an addition, and how?' and 'What if it were □ − 3 = 5 instead of 5 = □ − 3 — would the answer change?'
Show how you'd check that your answer to 8 + ? = 11 makes the sentence true.
activities.insight: Articulating the reasoning surfaces whether a child is using a keyword/positional habit or genuinely reasoning from which quantity is missing.

activities.title: Anchor each position to an operation (worked bar models)
steps: Study a worked part-whole/bar diagram for each unknown position (result, change, start, answer-left) with the missing segment highlighted.
Reveal, for each, which operation finds the missing part and why (whole − part = part; part + part = whole).
Then solve matching fresh equations and verify by substitution.
activities.insight: Each position maps to a specific inverse move once you identify the whole and the parts; the diagram makes that mapping visible.

checkQuestion: Solve these three and write the missing number in each box, working at the table while I watch: 8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □.
checkAnswer: ? = 3; □ = 8; □ = 12. Watch for the child using the inverse (11 − 8 = 3; 5 + 3 = 8) on the first two and adding directly on the last, and for correct handling of the answer-left/subtraction-position form.
